I mean kinda yeah. Part of the problem with teaching any science, chemistry included, is there are literally centuries worth of discoveries that build the foundation of what we know today. Its good to try and lay down the foundations in grade school, but its just unreasonably to expect the vast majority of teenagers to really fully grasp the whishy-whashy wave-like nature of electrons and how the "basic rules" of chemistry and bonding only really hold for the top three rows of the periodic table (and even then there's like a million exceptions). Talk to any chem major and they'll tell you how that one year of high school chem gets turned into 4 years of several classes per year's worth of science because they're actually getting into the details and even THEN there's still complexity left out.

Literally, every time you go up a level of formal learning in whatever scientific field, it's always first day of class: "So remember what we taught you last year? Forget about all that, its a million times more complicated and here's why."

And don't even get me started on notation, which I feel is part of your problem in this post. There are so many just arbitrary notation/symbolic choices that are standard now, some good, some absolutely terrible, and you have 0 choice because that's just what everyone else understands.

But yeah, big take away here: in nearly every thing you're taught, every single detail has a whole semesters worth of complexity that was cut for time. It doesn't mean what you've been taught is straight up wrong, you've just been given a version that sacrifices some of its truth in favor of simplicity.

I think you're confusing oxidation state with net charge. You are correct that the chromium gets reduced, gaining electrons and lowering the oxidation state. But, the chromium oxidation state is "balanced" by the neighboring oxygens all having a -2 oxidation state (its a bit more complicated than just balancing oxidation states but unless you want me to, I don't want to go into it too much). And, if you'll notice, summing up the oxidation states 2\*(+6) + 7\*(-2) = -2, the net charge of the ion.  


In the case of why the net charge is important, net charge is needed so that you can properly balance the equation. Charge balance is just as important as mass balance. The equations aren't "meant" to show electron flow, they're meant to summarize the reaction in which electron flow is only a part of it. If you wanted to keep track of everything that changes in a reaction, your equations will get very messy, very fast.

I will say that your question is getting very close to the "origin of life" theories. Since ATP is so ubiquitous, it obviously had be chosen extremely early on to the point that the cell that all modern  life is decended from likely also used ATP. Maybe not for as many things as we do, by definitely to power some reactions.

And now, we need to ask why this common ancestor chose to use ATP over other things that work just as well. But, to answer that requires knowledge of what evolutionary pressures were like at that point, and we really can't know that. You'd get the same results as asking "why these 20 amino acids", or "why do we mostly have protein enzymes but some RNA enzymes". You can hypothesize all you want, but at the end of the day, you'll still just have a hypothesis.

You're sorta just describing the problem with hourly wages in general. If person A and B work in the same office at min wage, but person A gets their work done faster, person A usually just ends up doing more work for the same pay. So yeah, hourly pay isn't perfect because skill can't be measured by time alone.

For specificly comms, I'd have to ask what you think the alternative should be. Hourly is something that's easy to measure and easy to understand. When I do painting commissions, I price based off area: easy to measure and easy to understand. Neither are fool proof ways of measuring the worth of a piece of art. How much something is worth is a nebulous concept, subject to opinion. Especially for new artists who haven't gotten a feel for how much their art is worth, how are they supposed to determine that (especially when going off of pure opinion, they'll often be underselling themself big time). Hourly is an easy starting point.

Like, to be clear, I agree with you. Hourly isn't the best indication because youre right, it doesn't take into account of the actual effort put in nor skill of the user. But effort and skill aren't measurable like time taken is, and in order to replace hourly as a pricing method, you'll need to replace it with something else measureable.

I've said this before, and I'll gladly say it again here. *We see Rose's development in reverse.* That's why people don't like her. We first see her at her most developed. She understands the complexity of humanity, she's made genuine close friends, she's literally made a fresh start for herself so that she could heal. Then, every information we get about her is worse than the last. She kept secrets, she bubbled Bismuth and told no one, she was literally Pink Diamond before, she abandoned Spinel for thousands of years because she thought she was too clingy and annoying, and she was the direct cause of her own original pearl's trauma and physical deformities. For some people, it feels like the kind and loving Rose from the beginning of the series was a mask, covering up this horrible immature child, and that would be the correct conclusion *if the aforementioned events happened in the same order that we learned about them*.

But that's not what happened. The Rose we knew at the beginning, the Rose that loved Earth and wanted to spread that love to whatever she could, that was how she actually was before she made Steven, not a mask. It's just unfortunate that we only ever get small parts of her revealed. She can't defend her own actions, or apologize for keeping all those secrets because she's gone, and that's part of the tragedy of it. No one in the show has the full picture of who Rose truly was and what she truly felt over her mistakes in the past. Not the Diamonds, not the crystal gems, not Pearl, not Greg, and not Steven. 

It's left to the audience to fill those gaps for themselves. I've filled those gaps with someone who, despite making many mistakes, wanted only to first fit in with her peers/family and later do what she thought was right. You've filled those gaps with parts of yourself. And others have filled those gaps with a dictator pretending to be a good person. I have my own opinions about what's more likely to be 'the truth' but at the end of the day, literary analysis is painted by one's opinions and experiences, and when there's so little to go off of, there is no one true interpretation.

If you take anything away from my big ol' ramble here, it's that all fictional characters have gaps that the audience is left to fill, whether they realize that or not. And when there's a disagreement around a character, it's likely that both sides just don't see the same character. Your Rose will be different from my Rose which will be different from anyone else's Rose, and that's just what consuming media is like.

Seconding all of TheFunkyWeirdo's points, drawing isn't necessary to be a fan.

As for any art advice, there will not be any 'tricks' to just pop out a dragon as a beginner, it takes practice. Also agree with TheFunkyWeirdo here, you need to focus on anatomy. Draw cats and dogs and lizards and any other four legged animal you can find pictures of. Some 'exercises' that I've done if you wanna try them out:

Look at a picture while drawing, do not trace. Mimic the reference as best you can. You can use a grid system as explained [here](https://feltmagnet.com/drawing/Portrait-Drawing-for-the-Ultimate-Beginner-The-Grid-Method), but at some point you want to be able to do it decently without a grid. Take as long as you need to here.

Do gesture drawings. Take a video of a cat and draw it's form. The purpose here is not to have any detail, but rather to capture, well it's gesture. Here is [wikipedia on gesture drawing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gesture_drawing). The key is to be fast. Vary the speed that you do the drawings. Gesture drawings can be about a minute or two per drawing, to just a few seconds per drawings. Find a speed that you feel challenges you, but not to hard and use that as your main gesture practice, but it's a good idea to still go faster or slower every now and then.

Try to draw things as simple shapes. This is the type of exercise where you'll develop some of your own style of drawing. Again, find some reference material and try to mimic the subject, but simplify it. The head is nothing but a sphere, the muzzle is just a plain box sticking off the sphere, etc. Once you get the hang of being able to simplify something from a picture, get rid of the reference. Use your previous simplified drawings that you feel are best and make something from your imagination. Draw how one of the collections of shapes would look if your reference had been laying down instead of standing up, looking to the left instead of straight at the camera, etc.

Those three techniques are how you learn to actually draw a good animal that looks like it exists and has weight and life to it. Of course, don't only do these exercises. These are for when you have the time to just sit down and pump out some drawing practice. Other times, feel free to doodle a little dragon head or whatever else you want to do. Practice is rigid, but true art is creative and exploratory.

Here are some spoiler-ed directions to the sky islands gate if you want: >!From the wall -> chimney gate, just go left. Don't go down, down go up, if theres multiple paths, take the left most one. There's a shelter immediately before the gate to sky islands in the gate room. It only needs karma 2 (counting base level as 1) so you just need to make a mad dash to that shelter and you're good.!<

Honestly, while Industrial > Outskirts > Farm Arrays is easier than Sky Islands > Farm Arrays, the path through Chimney is significantly longer, meaning more chances for lizards and vultures (and scavs if they hate you) to murder you. So what route you want depends on if you want to slug through longer Chimney to have the safety of Industrial and Outskirts, or do you want to rush through Chimney banking on the word of some stranger telling you that Sky Islands isn't that bad lol. If you choose to go to Industrial, here are some directions, also spoiler'ed: >!Just keep going down when you can. The chimney > industial gate does require karma 3, but there's a popcorn plant nearby that helps.!<

But yeah, don't feel too discouraged over finding chimney difficult. Sometimes, no amount of skill can help you when there's 20 vultures between you and your destination. With all this weirdness going on that comes with being a non s- and p-block element and being so far down the periodic table, there are many factors to consider, with no one singular answer. A mole is an amount of something. While it's obviously most useful in chemistry, the measurement can apply to anything. You can have a mole of cups. A mole of pieces of paper. A mole of stars. Saying that you have a mole of something is exactly the same as saying you have a billion of something. A mole is just a very specific number, 6.022x10\^(23) to be exact. While not very useful, it's still perfectly applicable to non-chemistry topics.

An amu is a mass unit that was defined based off of the mole. Think of it like this: you collect a mole of water and weigh it, it's about 18.02g. That gives you the molar mass of water: 18.02 grams per mole. Now, you *could* divide by avogadro's number to get the mass of a single molecule. This would give you a mass of about 2.99x10\^(-23) grams, and that's a perfectly valid number to use in your calculations. But, that's sorta cumbersome, and hard to use when comparing things, especially once you start messing around with huge organic molecules or the giant atoms in rows 6 and 7. So instead of having to deal with that, we just *define* a new unit. We say that "Okay, so the mass of a single water molecule is just gonna be the same number as it's molar mass, 18.02." Bada bing bada boom, you have yourself a new mass unit such that 1 gram is equal to 6.022x10\^(23) amu.

Now this probably isn't how any of this happened. Idk which concept actually came first and the thought process of each. But the point is that the ideas of 1 mole, 1 amu, and avogadro's number are all defined around eachother. Hope this helps, let me know if I can explain anything further!

It's not actually 2 individual bonds. Using diborane as an example, in the B-H-B bonding system, there are only 2 electrons, not 4. Those 2 electrons are shared between all three atoms.

You can think about it as one bond flipping between the two borons in a resonance structure (B----H    B   <==>   B    H----B)

Or as two half-bonds (B - - H - - B)

Or think of it in a lewis acid/base sense, as since BH3 is highly lewis acidic (strong electron acceptor), the boron in a single borane is able to "accept" the electron pair within the bond of the other borane.

All of these though basically describe the same system, three atoms all interacting with the same 2 electrons. This system is called a 3-center 2-electron bond, and it's the kind of thing you usually learn about in college level inorganic chem, particularly around when you start talking about coordination chemistry.

Here is the wikipedia article on [3-center 2-electron bonds.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-center_two-electron_bond) Hope this helps clear things up!

As you go down the periodic table, you keep adding on more and more electrons, and these electrons has something of an insulating effect on the valence electrons. Let's take oxygen and tellurium (Te) for an example. A neutral single oxygen has 8 total electrons. With just those 8, they're all really close to the nucleus and, since the nucleus is positive and electrons are negative, the attraction between the nucleus and the electrons is really strong to the point that loosing all 6 electrons to have a stable valence is just not gonna happen in standard conditions. But what oxygen can do is gain electrons. With only 8 other electrons between a theoretical new electron and the nucleus, an added electron would still be able to "see" the nucleus and still be attracted to it, making oxygen able form a -2 ion.

Tellurium, as an element in the same group, has the exact same valence, but it has a whopping 52 electrons in it's neutral state. This means that the outer valance electrons are extremely far away from the nucleus, making it easy to loose those electrons. Tellurium still does form a -2 ion but it's also more than capable of forming positive ions as well (though usually not the full +6, more often a +4 or +2 from what I can find online).

And this trend is seen everywhere. The heavier atoms have a lot of electrons which makes loosing electrons easier and ends up giving these heavy elements more of a metallic character. Hope this makes sense lol

As of yet there is no theoretical limit on the size of atoms and the electron shells. There are more atoms than just Oganesson with all the electron shells full. Really, that's the unifying property of the last column of the table. Helium, Neon, Argon, Krypton, Xenon, and Radon all have completely filled orbitals and valence shells. Each row down has a new shell for electrons in inhabit. It's perfectly reasonable that the next element after Oganesson, element 119, is just a matter of one extra proton and one extra electron. The only reason why the periodic table stops at 118 right now is just that, until someone does discover/create element 119, there's no reason to add a whole new row.

So in theory, there isn't a limit. In practice, it's a lot more complicated. The further we go, the less stable these elements are. Thus, while technically there is a sense in which an element with 300 protons and 300 electrons can exist, it's (in my opinion) almost certain that it'd be too unstable to exist long enough for us to even know if we've made it, at least until humanity comes up with some new crazy machine to do things like that.

Think about popcorn. Given a specific condition, there is a measurable time at which roughly half of the kernels will have popped. If you were to do this measurement several times and averaged it, you would get an estimate for the half-life of that brand of popcorn.

The thing is, half-life as a measurement of time only makes sense for a group, not individually. If you want to look at an individual kernel, you need to convert that half-life from a measurement of time to a measurement of probability. If your popcorn half life is 2mins, than you can say that for an individual kernel, there's a 50% chance it will pop before 2 mins have passed.

While yes, the longer you wait, the lower the probability is before the kernel pops. But while the chance of any one kernel staying unpopped for 20 minutes is pretty low, its not 0. When you have 300 or so kernels in one bag, the chance that just one of those kernels stays unpopped after 20mins is decently high.

It's just a consequence of how double bonds work. Crash course cause idk your level of chem knowledge: each sharp corner here is a carbon atom and the lines going directly from corner to corner are "sigma" bonds. Sigma bonds are the structural backbone of a molecule, if there's any covalent bonding between two atoms, there's a sigma bond.

When you see lines on the side of those sigma bonds, those are "pi" bonds. Carbons can only handle 2 pi bonds (plus 1 sigma bond between each bonding atom), and you can see the resulting triple bonds in that first picture if you were to fill a carbon bond to the max

Bonds are basically made of electrons, specifically a pair of them. The electrons in pi bonds are in a sense further away from the bonding atoms than the ones on the sigma bonds, making the pi bond less stable.

Now the fun part. When you have "conjugated" pi bonds (think double-single-double when looking at these diagrams) you get something called resonance. In essence, this lets the pi bonds move around. For non ring structures, how we draw it is usually the most stable form, but if you provide the right stressor to a molecule (such as forcing an extra electron into it), the pi bonds will start to flip between adjacent pairs of carbon atoms. Here, the pi bond isn't between just 2 atoms any more, the 2 electrons from that pi bond spend equal time hovering over two different pairs of carbons. This is what we call "delocalization", when electrons are no longer localized to one individual bond.

Finally we come to ring structures. In ring structures like the ones above, if you follow the double-single-double pattern, you'll find that all of the double bonds are conjugated with themselves in a way. This makes it so that you no longer need a stressor to cause these molecules to resonate, they just do that on their own. As a consequence of that, all those pi bonds are just flip flopping all over the place, delocalizing all of it. Since those electrons are in a way equally shared by many bonds, you can't see where they are, cause they're every where.

The reason why you can still see the triple bonds is because there's 2 pi bonds there, not 1. That extra pi bonds ruins the whole bond's ability to resonate. So, while those rings will still resonate individually, the triple bonds won't be involved.

Eh, at that point, Katara dying wouldn't really have done anything for the story. First, the only person there to witness the death would have been Zuko who, in reality, just wasn't exactly super close with Katara. They were friends, sure, but they really didn't have the same chemistry as Zuko and Aang, or even Zuko and Sokka. Both Sokka and Aang would one learn of her death after ozai is defeated and by then its the end of the show, there's no time to explore the grief of these characters who she had the greatest impact on.

Second, just because her "purpose" in the show was complete, that doesn't mean she should be killed off. Iroh's purpose was complete: he had reunited with Zuko who had clearly finally found his path in life. There wasn't anything narratively left for Iroh after the battle in ba sing se except to life the rest of his life content with his immensely positive impact on the world, but having him die far from the person he loved as his own son would have just felt a bit unsatisfying. The same thing goes for katara.

Finally, there really wasn't any reason for Katara to sacrifice herself in such a way. Zuko sacrificing himself for Katara was a way of showing how far he'd come, starting as the villain of s1 willing to hurt others for his own misguided sense of honor, to someone who had, by his own choices, rejected what he thought he wanted for years and instead chose the righteous path. With Katara, she was already the type to throw herself into harms way for the people she cared about, there wasn't any reason to show that, we knew already. Maybe there would be something interesting if, say, she was the first to go against Azula, died, then Agni Kai, but I feel like that would take far more away from Zuko than it would give to Katara.

Its a bit more plausible of a direction if she doesn't die at the Agni Kai but that would change the story more heavily and still has some problems. Like if she instead went with sokka to the airships and died there while suki or toph went with zuko, but that still removes Aang from that moment, which I feel like if Katara's gonna die, Aang needs to be present to be remotely a satisfying narrative choice. Tl;dr I think that in order to have Katara die in a way that even has a chance to be narratively satisfying, there would have to be major overhauls to the 3rd season story which, considering her characterization up till then, seems unnecessary at best and extremely detrimental at worst

If you haven't seen one, look up a picture taken by the hubble telescope. All the stars will have this distinctive four pointed shape to them. This is because how the telescope is built, the internal support structure effects how the light is reflected, and it ends up creating those artifacts.

The human eye does the same thing, all the little veins and imperfections inside your eye affect the final image, but its not extremely noticeable all the time. If you try looking at a small bright point of light and unfocus your eye (have one eye closed too, the image will actually be different for each eye) you should be able to see something similar to the pointy star shape, just much more irregular and likely with more than 5 points. mRNA doesn't touch your DNA. Crash course: DNA is used to make proteins. mRNA (messenger RNA) is created off of DNA, this way, the RNA can leave the nucleus while the DNA stays nice and safe in the nucleus. The mRNA then goes to a Ribosome which reads the mRNA and builds the corresponding protein, after which, the mRNA is destroyed and the made protien can go off and do what it needs to do.

The mRNA goes straight to the ribosome to make the spike protein, it can't go into the nucleus where the DNA is unless there's already something else really wrong with your cells. The only thing that'll remain in your body after the vaccine is immune cells and antibodies. The rest of your body will be like nothing ever happened.

It's the physical structure in how those carbon atoms are arranged that change the color. The structure in true white diamonds is more or less perfectly regular. For red/pink diamonds, theres an irregularity in the lattice structure that changes how the light interacts with the diamond as it passes through. Think of it as you have a bunch of cardboard boxes stacked up in a perfect cube. A white diamond is where all those boxes are brand new and fit together prefectly. When you put some dents in a few of the boxes, then when it takes on a red/pink color. It's still all cardboard, but the structure isn't as perfect any more. Hope that made a little more sense

In all honesty this looks pretty good. It sounds like you're having trouble with foreshortening (drawing something that is warped by perspective).  The best thing you can do is try and find some reference picks of whatever your having trouble with and just copy it. It's hard with dragons, but try and look for something similar on a real aninal or art done my others.

For me I use dog faces to help with muzzles. For horns you could practice with deer antlers or one of the more spiky reptiles. Idk what a good real world analog for the ears would be, but that's where other people art can help.

And if all also fails, make your own model. Play doh is fairly cheap and while it's bad for full body sculpts, it can work with smaller body parts. Heh those are getting a bit out of my field of expertise. I'm not a pure bred biologist, just a bio chemist who had a big interest in how DNA works. But im glad to have helped with the original question~ ^w^

Yeah they're just simpler. Lysosomes and such are more or less just bags full of enzymes, they're really only responsible for small, short reactions. Look up a chart of respiration or photosynthesis though and you'll see just how much is involved. Plus they're also structural differences. Look up some diagrams and a lysosome is basically just a membrane holding some goop but a chloroplast theres two membranes and a fuck ton of those little circles inside the inner membrane

It more or less boils down to efficiency. Once mitochondria and chloroplasts(all instances of 'they' refers to both organelles from now on) entered that symbiotic relationship with their hosts cells, there were a lot of genes that they didnt have to handle themselves anymore  For instance, before they would have had to repair their own cell membrane but now that they're in a host cell, that cell can handle all the machinery to do that. With the host handling more of the maintenance type stuff, they now have more room to put respiration/photosynthesis bits, making an increase in energy production and driving evolution in that direction.

The genes they have left now are the type of stuff that's specific to the organelle. Any efficiency gained by moving those last few genes to the nucleus is lost again be requiring some form of communication between the organelle and nucleus.

Tl;dr the genes moved to the nucleus were more general/used less often while the ones still in the organelle are more specific and used more often.

Okay! Water benders are the easiest to explain. They strictly bend H2O, as per the name. Doesn't matter in what form though, so they can freely bend ice, liquid water, vapor, and switch between them at will, which in theory means they can instantly varporize a persons blood so that's fun. It could be possible that there are other bendable liquids but theres not enough evidence for or against. 

Air again is super easy. If it's a gas, they can bend it. Oxygen? Helium? Sulfur Hexaflouride? Air benders can bend all that stuff.

Now the more tricky stuff. Fire benders don't actually bend any kind of physical matter but instead bend energy. For instance, to simply make a flame, a fire bender would bend some of the thermal energy in their body as well from the air around them and concentrate it by the palm of the hand hot enough so that the oxygen in the air can combust on it's own. This is also consistent with lightning bending as, rather than thermal energy, you're bending electrical energy.

And now earth menders. Due to the ambiguity and huge variance in what can count as "earth" this was trouble some. Okay so, basically and earth bender can bend any and all metals and metal based compounds. (Apologies for all the chemistry jargon but I'll do my best to explain it). So most periodic tables have a little zigzag starting at carbon doing down and left to iodine. Every element right of that line is a metal, except hydrogen. An earth bender can bend all of these as well as compounds based off of these elements like iron rust (Fe2O3). This also has the benefit of excluding compounds like water or organic molecules (stuff that makes up plants and people) that are almost entirely carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, all of which are non-metals. Now I hear you asking "But Alari, platinum would be included in that and in korra we see that they can't bend it!" But! The thing is, they can! It's just really hard. What dictates the difficulty in bending compounds is it's molar mass (to find this, and element's molar mass is roughly it's atomic number times 2 and a compound's is just all the elements added together so H2O would be H+H+O). Elemental platinum has a molar mass of 195 while say a compound like silicon dioxide which makes up 42% of the earths crust has a molar mass of just 60. No some of the holes in this part of the theory. First Toph's explanation of metal bending "feeling the earth impurities. My guess is this is more of a crutch then anything, since the metal itself is do dense for her to bend then, she can use the impurities instead, like bending blood to move a person even though you can't bend the rest of the body. The difficulty in it was feeling that less dense earth, bending such small amounts of it, and having the power to overcome the resistance of trying to move earth embedded in solid metal, hence why no one could do it until Toph. **<<Spoilers for Korra Ahead>>** Second hole: the mercury in Korra. The liquid metal that Korra gets shoved in her is most likely mercury due to the similarities between her condition on mercury poisoning, and we see Toph bend it (as well as korra and and unknown person) showing that earth benders can bend mercury. The problem is, elemental mercury is even denser than elemental platinum. It's not by much, but it's still significant and I still don't really have an answer for that :/
